newsitem.title: UK: Half Britain's coalmines could close - group.
newsitem.headline: Half Britain's coalmines could close - group.

text.p: A group representing British coalminers said on Monday it believed half of the country's 29 collieries would have to close in the next five years unless a new government takes urgent steps to save them.
Nearly 100 mines have closed in Britain since 1990 when the Conservative government announced plans to privatise the coalmining industry.

The Coalfield Communities Campaign (CCC) said that still more are under threat because of unfair competition from the nuclear and gas industries and due to new environmental protection guidelines calling for cuts in sulphur emissions.

Apparently assuming the opposition Labour Party would take power at Britain's next eleciton, due to be held by May 22, the CCC urged Labour to carry out a series of measures to try to save the industry.

"A new Labour government must be made aware of the seriousness of the distortions that still exist in the energy market. A fair deal for coal is no more than we ask," CCC chairman Bill Flanagan told a room packed with journalists and miners in the town of Pontefract, northern England.

The town lies at the heart of a once thriving coalmining community and the scene of ferocious demonstrations during the year-long miners' strike in 1984-85. Now the area is riddled with unemployment and associated social problems. The CCC urged Labour, far ahead in opinion polls, to review what it called "sweetheart" deals tying electricity generators to buying gas.

It wants a review of the cost of running ageing nuclear power stations, investment in clean-coal technology and an end to plans to use orimulsion and petroleum coke, which it described as "the two dirtiest fuels of all".
The organisation said it also wants a new government to review the time limits set for cutting sulphur emissions from power stations, which it said are impossible for the coal industry to meet.

A spokesman for RJB Mining, which bought all surviving coal mines in England when they were privatised in 1992, denied the future looked as bleak as the CCC predicted but said the company backed the campaign.
"We are pleased to be able to join CCC in calling for a fair deal for the coal industry," RJB marketing director Colin Godfrey told the meeting.
The CCC has an impressive record in predicting the fate of Britain's diminished coal-mining industry. In 1990 it said 41 pits would close in the run-up to privatisation. In fact 45 closed.

Two years later it said a "dash for gas", which followed the repeal of the European Union directive that banned the use of natural gas to fuel power stations, would result in the loss of more than 20 collieries.
Later that year, the government announced that 31 would close causing a furore among both miners and the public.
